Your report will appear here.

Common questions

Does this tell me whether my site is GDPR or CCPA compliant?

No. It only reports observable differences between two trace exports you supply — requests added or removed and storage keys added or removed. The generated record says explicitly that it does not determine compliance; that judgment needs a person who knows your legal basis and traces from every relevant browser and region.

What exactly gets compared — just requests and storage keys?

Yes, and only what's in the trace JSON: each request's URL and method, and each storage entry's key. Cookie values, third-party pixels the trace didn't capture, in-memory state, and anything that happened outside the capture window are invisible to this comparison.

Do the before and after traces have to be the same site?

Yes, if both traces include a site field — the tool refuses to compare a before-trace from one site against an after-trace from another. Omit the field on either side and that check is skipped, so keeping site populated is what catches an accidental cross-site comparison.

Do the traces I paste in get uploaded anywhere?

No. Comparison happens entirely in this browser tab; nothing is sent anywhere. Prefer working from real captured traffic instead of hand-typed JSON? The HAR before/after diff takes raw DevTools exports the same way, locally.

Consent Change Record

Did that consent banner actually stop the tracking requests, or just hide the banner? Export two HAR network captures from your browser — one before a consent choice, one after — and this diffs every request and cookie that appeared or disappeared. Nothing is uploaded.

How to get a HAR file

Open your browser's DevTools → Network tab → reload the page → make your consent choice (or don't) → right-click any request → "Save all as HAR". Do this twice on the same site: once before the consent action, once after, then drop both files below. Only test sites you own or are authorized to test.

Compare two captures

Diff report

Third-party requests present in both captures

These carried on across the consent choice — the same endpoint was requested before and after. This is usually the part of the report worth reading first: a request that disappears is easy to spot, but one that never stopped is what a consent check is looking for. Repeats of the same endpoint are collapsed into one row. Requests to the page's own host are counted below rather than listed, because a site's own assets are expected to persist.

Cookies present in both captures

Requests that appeared or disappeared

Cookies that appeared or disappeared

The export is a dated JSON file with this exact diff, the two source filenames, and this disclaimer — a record for you to review, not a compliance determination.

vs-comparing-the-traces-by-eye.html.text:
← Consent Change Record

Consent Change Record vs. comparing the two traces by eye

Reading a before and after export side by side and checking which URLs show up in both is the default way to eyeball a consent change. It reliably misses a tracker that still fires, just fewer times -- because "still appears in both" and "unchanged" are not the same question. This free tool counts occurrences instead.

What comparing two traces by eye involves

Reviewing a consent sequence by hand usually means opening both exports and scanning the after trace for each URL that appeared before: is it still there? Gone? Something new? That works well for a tracker that either fires cleanly in both states or disappears entirely -- both are visible as presence or absence.

It works less well the moment a request fires more than once in one or both traces, which real trackers do routinely -- a pixel loaded once per page section, a script polling on an interval. A URL present three times before consent and once after is still, by a presence check, "in both traces" -- so it reads as unchanged, even though two of its three firings actually stopped. The reverse hides the opposite problem just as easily: a tracker that fired once before and started firing repeatedly after.

What mattersComparing the traces by eyeThis tool
A request that fires fewer times after consent, without disappearing entirely.Reads as unchanged -- the URL is present on both sides, and nothing draws the eye to how many times.Counts occurrences per request on each side and reports the surplus as removed.
A request that starts firing more often after consent.Same blind spot in reverse -- presence alone cannot distinguish once from repeatedly.Reports the extra occurrences as added, the same counting logic applied both ways.
A storage key that is genuinely new versus one that was already there.Usually visible -- a short list of keys is easy to scan for an unfamiliar name.Diffs storage keys the same way as requests, for consistency and a single exported record.
A source-linked record you can hand to someone else.Whatever notes the reviewer happens to write down.A downloadable report naming exactly which requests and storage keys changed, and by how much.

Comparing the traces by eye is not wrong -- it is how anyone reviewing a consent sequence starts, and it is right about anything that is purely present or purely absent. What it is not well suited to is a duplicate count, which is exactly the case a script that fires on an interval or per page section produces.

Open Consent Change Record to compare your own two traces.

The same worked example a presence check would pass

Before a visitor rejects analytics consent, an endpoint fires three times. After, it fires once more -- still present, just not three times:

BEFORE                                          AFTER
GET  cdn.example.test/app.js                    GET  cdn.example.test/app.js
POST analytics.example.test/collect             POST analytics.example.test/collect
POST analytics.example.test/collect             storage: consent_state, _ga
POST analytics.example.test/collect
storage: consent_state

Scanning the after trace for analytics.example.test/collect finds it -- it is right there, exactly as it was before. A presence check confirms "still fires" and moves on. Run this tool's own comparator (compareTraces) against the same two traces and it reports 2 removed requests to that URL (three before, one after -- two firings actually stopped) alongside one storage key added (_ga), with the request that still fires once correctly listed as unchanged, not as evidence nothing changed. Every figure here is asserted directly against the comparator's own output, not estimated.

Common questions

Isn't comparing two DevTools exports by eye enough?

It catches a request or storage key that is entirely new, or one that vanishes completely -- both stand out because the URL is simply present or absent. It works less well the moment a tracker fires more than once, which trackers routinely do (a pixel loaded once per section, a script polling on an interval). A URL that appears three times before consent and once after still 'appears in both traces' to a presence check, so it reads as unchanged -- even though two of its three firings actually stopped.

How easy is it really to miss a reduced-but-not-removed tracker by eye?

In this tool's own worked example, an analytics endpoint fires three times before a visitor rejects analytics consent and once after. Scanning the after trace for that URL finds it -- it is right there, so a reviewer confirms 'yes, this still fires' or 'no, nothing changed here' without counting instances. The correct finding is neither: two of the three firings stopped and one did not, which only shows up if you count occurrences on each side rather than checking presence.

Does this tool replace reviewing the traces myself?

No, and it only diffs the two trace files you give it -- it does not capture traces, crawl a site, or determine whether what it found is compliant with any law. Reviewing what a consent sequence should do in the first place is still your job. This tool exists for the specific, mechanical part of that review most likely to go wrong under a presence-only read: counting occurrences of each request and storage key correctly on both sides.

Already checked how this compares to a full consent management platform? See Consent Change Record vs. Cookiebot.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, privacy, or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. vs-cookiebot.html.text:
← Consent Change Record

Consent Change Record vs. Cookiebot

Different jobs: Cookiebot crawls a whole domain on a schedule, auto-detects trackers, and manages the banner that blocks them. This page compares two trace snapshots you already captured of one consent sequence and reports what actually changed — free, local, no account.

What each tool is for

Cookiebot, from Usercentrics, is a consent management platform (CMP). Its scanner crawls a site's pages on a recurring schedule, auto-detects and categorizes the cookies and trackers it finds against its own database, and generates a cookie declaration page. Its banner blocks third-party scripts from firing until a visitor consents, supports IAB TCF, and covers a whole domain as an ongoing subscription tier scaled to page count. It is sold as recurring software; its own pricing is not something this session can verify, so no figure for it is stated here.

This tool does none of that. It does not crawl a site, does not maintain a tracker database, and does not render or manage a consent banner. It takes exactly two inputs — a before and after JSON trace you already captured around one consent choice (the requests fired and the storage keys written in each state) — and reports what changed between them: which requests appear only after consent, which fire regardless, and which storage keys were added. Comparison runs in your browser tab; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool never contacts the site itself. There is no account, no scheduled crawl, and no per-domain subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it

I want automatic tracker detection and categorization across every page of my domain.Cookiebot or a comparable scanner — this tool has no crawler and no tracker database; it only diffs traces you supply.
Do I need to create an account, install a script tag, or pay per page scanned to use it?This tool: no, ever. Cookiebot is used through a subscription tied to a site's page count.

Most teams get different value from each: Cookiebot (or a comparable CMP) to build and run the banner and auto-block scripts across a whole site as a paid subscription, and a free tool like this one for a fast, private, source-linked answer to "what did this one consent sequence actually do" — useful on its own for a small agency, and useful as an independent spot check even for a site that already pays for a CMP.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the comparison runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or Cookiebot?

They do different jobs. Cookiebot (from Usercentrics) is a consent management platform: it crawls a site's pages on a recurring schedule, auto-detects and categorizes the cookies and trackers it finds, renders the consent banner itself, and blocks scripts from firing until a visitor consents, across a whole domain, sold as an ongoing subscription tier. This tool does not crawl anything, does not detect trackers on its own, and does not render or manage a banner. You paste two dated trace exports you already captured — one from before a consent choice, one from after — and it reports which requests and storage keys actually changed between them, entirely in your browser. A site that needs its consent banner built, its scripts auto-blocked, and its whole domain rescanned on a schedule is the case Cookiebot is built for. An agency or reviewer that already has two traces of one consent sequence and wants a fast, free, source-linked record of what that banner actually did is the case this tool is built for — including checking whether a Cookiebot-managed banner is blocking what it claims to.

what-did-my-cookie-banner-actually-chang.text:
← Consent Change Record

What did my cookie banner actually change?

The banner renders. The buttons work. The vendor dashboard is green. None of that answers the question a client or a reviewer actually asks: when someone declines, what stops happening?

Frequently the answer is "less than you think." Consent tooling is configured separately from the scripts it is meant to gate, so a tag added later by a marketing team, a script loaded by another script, or a vendor that ignores the consent signal keeps firing behind a perfectly correct banner — invisibly, because the interface is not where the failure shows.

Open the free consent change record

Compare two states, not one

Capture what the page does before the consent choice and again after it, then diff the two. What you want out of the comparison is:

  • Requests that appear only after consent — the ones the banner is genuinely gating.
  • Requests that appear in both states — the ones it is not.
  • Storage keys written either way — the quieter half of the same question.

A trace holds only metadata — url, method, and storage key values — plus the site, capture time, browser, and which sequence it is. That is enough to answer the question and deliberately not enough to carry page content.

How to use it

  1. Capture a before-consent and an after-consent trace of a site you own or are authorized to test.
  2. Paste both into the page and choose Compare traces. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account.
  3. Download the report as your dated review artifact.
  4. If you already have DevTools HAR captures instead, the sibling HAR comparison tool diffs two HAR files and groups known tracker domains.

What the record is, and is not

It is a dated, source-linked list of observable differences between two captures — useful in a client review, a handover, or a file you keep. It is not a compliance determination, and it does not claim a site is lawful under any privacy regime. The observations are the evidence; what they mean for your obligations is a question for a qualified professional.

Common questions

How do I check what my cookie banner actually changes?

Capture what the page does before the consent choice and again after it, then compare the two. Record the outbound requests and the storage keys written in each state and diff them. That comparison answers the question the banner's own screenshot cannot: which third-party requests only appear after consent, which appear regardless, and which storage keys are written either way. A banner that renders correctly and blocks nothing is a common and entirely invisible failure.

Why is a screenshot of the banner not enough?

A screenshot shows the interface, not the behaviour. Consent tooling is usually configured separately from the scripts it is supposed to gate, so a tag added later by a marketing team, a script loaded by another script, or a vendor that ignores the consent signal will keep firing behind a perfectly correct banner. Only observing the requests and storage in each state shows what the banner does.

Does this prove my site is compliant?

No. It produces a dated record of observable differences between two traces you captured — request URLs and methods, and storage keys. It is evidence for a review, not a compliance badge, and it makes no determination under any privacy law. Only test sites you own or are authorized to test, and take advice from a qualified professional on what the observations mean for your obligations.
